explanations.explanation: Brother is right. The message opens, "This is what your brother Israel says…" (Numbers 20:14). Moses reaches out family to family, and I think that's a smart way to knock on a door. It's like showing up with a fresh batch of cookies and saying, "It's me, your kin!" Hard to slam the door on that.
Servant isn't the word. Moses doesn't bow and scrape here. The message says, "This is what your brother Israel says…" (Numbers 20:14). Brother to brother, not servant to king.

Neighbor makes sense, since Israel's camped right at Edom's edge. But the message uses a closer word: "This is what your brother Israel says…" (Numbers 20:14). Moses doesn't say neighbor. He says brother, and that's a different kind of knock on the door.

Not quite, friend. The message says the opposite: "The Egyptians mistreated us and our fathers…" (Numbers 20:15). Mistreated is a long way from kindly. That's the hardship Moses wants Edom's king to know about.

False is right. The message says, "The Egyptians mistreated us and our fathers…" (Numbers 20:15). Kindly doesn't show up anywhere in that sentence. Moses tells it plainly so the king knows what Israel has walked through.

An angel is right. The message says that when they cried out, the LORD "…heard our voice, sent an angel, and brought us out of Egypt." (Numbers 20:16). They cried, and He heard. That's the whole story in one breath.

A raven is a fun guess, but it's not in this verse. The message says the LORD "…heard our voice, sent an angel, and brought us out of Egypt." (Numbers 20:16). A raven does bring bread to Elijah (1 Kings 17:6), but that's a different story. Here, the angel is who He sent.

A chariot of fire sounds like a big entrance, I'll give you that. But the verse says the LORD "…heard our voice, sent an angel, and brought us out of Egypt." (Numbers 20:16). No chariot is mentioned here. The angel is the one He sent.
Permission to pass through is right. The message says, "Please let us pass through your land." (Numbers 20:17). Israel isn't asking to move in. They just want to get through, and they say please.
Settling down isn't the ask. The message says, "Please let us pass through your land." (Numbers 20:17). Pass through, then keep going. No unpacking, no boxes, no moving truck.

Soldiers to march with them would be a whole different request, friend. The message asks, "Please let us pass through your land." (Numbers 20:17). Israel wants a way through, not an escort. I think asking a king for a road AND his army in one letter would be a lot, even with a please.

True! Israel says, "We will not go through any field or vineyard, or drink water from any well." (Numbers 20:17). Fields, vineyards, wells. They list it all, one by one, like a baker promising not to touch ONE crumb on the cooling rack. I'd have caved on the spot, friend. I can't even promise that about my own dough.

Not false, friend. The message says, "We will not go through any field or vineyard, or drink water from any well." (Numbers 20:17). Israel really does make that promise. It's a pretty polite way to ask for a road.

The King's Highway is right. Israel says, "We will stay on the King’s Highway; we will not turn to the right or to the left until we have passed through your territory." (Numbers 20:17). Straight through, no side trips. That's a promise you can picture.
The Way of the Sea is a road name, but it's not the one here. Israel says, "We will stay on the King’s Highway…" (Numbers 20:17). Same idea of staying put on the road, different road.

The road to Damascus is a different road, friend. It shows up when Saul travels toward that city (Acts 9:3). In this passage, Israel says, "We will stay on the King’s Highway; we will not turn to the right or to the left…" (Numbers 20:17). That's the road they name.

explanations.answer: No or they'll come out with the sword
explanations.explanation: That's right. Edom answers, "You may not travel through our land, or we will come out and confront you with the sword." (Numbers 20:18). Israel asked so nicely, and the answer is no with a sword attached. That one stings.

explanations.answer: Yes if Israel pays a toll first
explanations.explanation: A toll would've been a friendlier answer, friend. But Edom says, "You may not travel through our land, or we will come out and confront you with the sword." (Numbers 20:18). No toll booth here, just a no. Israel is the one who brings up paying, and that comes next.

explanations.answer: Yes but only through the desert
explanations.explanation: Edom doesn't give a yes at all. The answer is, "You may not travel through our land, or we will come out and confront you with the sword." (Numbers 20:18). No desert route offered. Just a flat no.

Pay is right, baker. Israel says, "…if we or our herds drink your water, we will pay for it." (Numbers 20:19). They're not asking for a handout, they're pulling out the wallet! Water for a whole herd, and they're offering to cover the bill. That's the kind of customer every shop owner prays for. I once got a quarter's worth of respect in my life, so I know what it's like when somebody offers to pay.
Wait isn't the word. Israel says, "…if we or our herds drink your water, we will pay for it." (Numbers 20:19). They're offering to pay, not to stand around. Waiting doesn't buy water.

Prayer is never a bad idea, friend, but it's not the word in this verse. Israel says, "…if we or our herds drink your water, we will pay for it." (Numbers 20:19). They're offering to hand over payment for the water.

True! Israel says, "There will be no problem; only let us pass through on foot." (Numbers 20:19). Hear that "only"? That's the whole ask. No fields, no vineyards, just feet on the road. I've seen bakers ask for more than that when they want one extra cookie, and I still said yes.
Not false, friend. Israel says, "There will be no problem; only let us pass through on foot." (Numbers 20:19). That "only" is the whole ask. Walking through is all they want.

explanations.answer: They come out with a large army
explanations.explanation: That's right. Edom "…came out to confront the Israelites with a large army and a strong hand." (Numbers 20:20). Two nos, then an army. Israel asked politely twice and got a crowd of soldiers for it.

explanations.answer: They send gifts out to Moses
explanations.explanation: No gifts, friend. The text says Edom "…came out to confront the Israelites with a large army and a strong hand." (Numbers 20:20). That's a very different kind of delivery than a gift basket.

Not quite, friend. Edom said, "You may not pass through." and then "…came out to confront the Israelites with a large army and a strong hand." (Numbers 20:20). The text tells us Edom refused Israel passage. Nobody is waving them down that road.

Not this time, friend. The passage ends, "…Edom refused to allow Israel to pass through their territory, and Israel turned away from them." (Numbers 20:21). Israel turns away, and they don't fight their way through. Sometimes walking away is the move.

False is right. The passage ends, "…Edom refused to allow Israel to pass through their territory, and Israel turned away from them." (Numbers 20:21). Israel turns away. No fighting through, even with that army standing right there.
